newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS - Australian profit upturn seen after dismal 95/96.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - Australian profit upturn seen after dismal 95/96.

text.p: Australian companies finished off a disappointing annual earnings season last week, but profits are expected to recover in 1997 from 18 months of declining growth as the market nears a low in its earnings cycle.
"The profit reporting season has been pretty disappointing overall," said Susan Creighton, an economist at brokers ABN AMRO Hoare Govett.

Analysts said local industrial firms reported an average earnings fall of about 10 percent in 1995/96 (July-June), while resource-based groups posted a 12 percent drop, making it the first annual average profit fall since the 1990/91 recession.
Slower economic growth, higher taxes, weak metals prices and a stronger local currency were blamed for the profit falls.
Creighton, however, said she expected steady earnings growth to emerge in 1996/97 .
Australia's low annual inflation rate of about three percent contributed to the deterioration in profit margins, making it more difficult to pass on higher costs to customers.
"This is the first time we have had one and a half years of earnings downgrades in a soft landing economic environment," said John Banos, an equity strategist at McIntosh Barings.

Despite the disappointments, there were strong profit performers and generous dividend payments from gambling group Tabcorp Holdings Ltd, insurer QBE Insurance Ltd and the Commonwealth Bank of Australia.
"Actually it hasn't been all that horrendous, as many companies have flagged the earnings problems this year," said Robert Credaro, equities strategist at broker Macquarie Equities.

The nation's largest public company, resources and steel giant the Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd, set the tone of the mainly grim earnings crop when it delivered a 1995/96 annual profit well below market expectations on June 28, analysts said.
Other companies to disappoint include food group Burns, Philp & Co Ltd, engineer Australian National Industries Ltd and building materials supplier Boral Ltd.

However, Australian companies are expected to record an average profit rise of about 10 percent in the 1996/97 year as economic growth starts to pick up pace in calendar 1997, along with a long awaited turnaround in the depressed housing market.
"Coming into calendar 1997, we would expect a slightly better environment, but I think in the near term it is still very slow," said J.B. Were's head of research Craig Drummond.
"There is no doubt that the housing cycle is near the bottom as is the profit cycle for most industrial firms. Potentially there is still a bit more pain in the next six months," he said.
"There are quite a few companies talking about reducing labour, that is never a good sign."
Australian state-owned telecommunications group Telstra Corp said on Friday it would cut a further 13,000 jobs on top of the already announced 9,000 staff cuts, over the next three years.
But Telstra also announced a record Australian corporate profit of A$2.30 billion (US$1.83 billion) in 1995/96, up 31.5 percent on the previous year.

However, despite the generally expected earnings rebound in 1996/97, profits for resource groups and exporters would continue to suffer if the Australian dollar remained at its current levels of around US$0.80 cents, analysts said.
The Australian dollar was around $0.73 cents at the start of 1996 and about $0.70 cents in July 1995.

"If it does sustain 80 (U.S.) cents or above that level most of next year, that of course will have a downward impact on the earnings of those companies that are exposed to offshore, such as the resources," said Creighton from ABN AMRO.
